zod-4-6-6-compromised-by-malware.background: Security researchers flagged a suspicious commit in Zod 4.6.6 that added a pre‑install script to download and execute external code, but the change was reverted before the npm package was published, leaving the released version clean. The incident prompted a review of the library’s commit history and confirmed no malicious payloads were included in the published 4.6.6 tarball. Separately, the @tanstack/zod‑adapter package was compromised in a 2026 supply‑chain attack linked to the Mini Shai‑Hulud campaign, where a hijacked npm maintainer account pushed malware that stole credentials and propagated to other packages. The attack underscored the need for credential rotation and dependency hygiene in projects that rely on Zod adapters. Developers should stay on patched version and audit adapters for integrity.

fingerprints-are-the-new-cookies.title: Fingerprints are the new cookies
fingerprints-are-the-new-cookies.content:
## From now on I’ll call you:

…

computing…

Try refreshing the page. Clear the cookies. Connect to a VPN.

You’re still the **…**.

Now open it on your phone or some other device and your nickname will be different and just as consistent.

Is it different in incognito? Good. But it’s always the same? Bad news.

**Imagine this:**

Most websites you visit get paid to show ads and indirectly run my script that lets me know you’re the …. I can use it to decide what ads you’ll see. But more importantly, if you’ve made an account on that website, I can offer to buy your data - whatever they can share under their privacy policy: your name, activity, conversations with AI…

Pretty soon I’d know more about you [than your friends do](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1418680112) - perhaps more than you know yourself.

### “So what?” - you say.

> “I have nothing to hide. And I prefer my ads to be relevant… sometimes they show me exactly what I need! And the data is anonymised anyway…”

See, the thing is, it’s not about you at all. It’s not really about the ads anymore either. Nobody cares about you. And if the police or your government happen to care, I’ll gladly take their money too.

I look at all this data and I don’t see people. I see patterns. Patterns emerging out of patterns. A living, digital fractal state of the economy, society and human psyche. The crystal ball of the 21st century and it’s made of silicon! **That’s** the product.

**And to the highest bidder it goes!**

What does that make you then? A gear? An ox? A volunteer?

* * *

Remember the big fuss about third-party cookies? It was so big that the EU had already rolled out one of its greatest inventions - consent banners.

If EU ships faster than tech companies, that can only mean the tech companies are sitting on their hands. And one of those tech companies happens to hold two-thirds of the browser market.

What was the play?

Let’s give it up for Google - the biggest ad company on Earth!

**ACT I. PRESSURE** - [“PRIVACY IS PARAMOUNT TO US, IN EVERYTHING WE DO.”](https://blog.google/products-and-platforms/products/chrome/building-a-more-private-web/)

It’s 2019 and the cookies are still hot. It’s become bad PR and Safari and Firefox already block them.

A year later Google pledges: we will destroy cookies!! And establish a new, privacy-first reign.

**ACT II. DISTRACTION** - [“INSTEAD OF DEPRECATING THIRD-PARTY COOKIES, WE WOULD INTRODUCE A NEW EXPERIENCE”](https://privacysandbox.google.com/blog/privacy-sandbox-update)

5 years later: people are now preoccupied with far greater worries than cookies, and the solutions Google has developed (Privacy Sandbox) kinda suck and have raised antitrust concerns so nobody uses them.

“You know what, let’s just keep the cookies. We’ll mask your IP address* though!” (* but only when incognito while authenticated) (** in the end they didn’t even deliver on that)

**ACT III. ACCELERATION** - [YOU CAN NOW USE DEVICE FINGERPRINTING IN OUR AD PRODUCTS](https://privacymatters.dlapiper.com/2025/01/googles-u-turn-on-device-fingerprinting-icos-response-and-subsequent-guidance/)

Now there’s a better way to know who’s who!

## How does fingerprinting work?

Nice, let’s nerd out properly.

You visit a website. Your browser sends a request to the server and the server returns code for the browser to run.

The request already reveals information about you; what browser you use, the language it’s in, the OS that runs it and your IP address, which the server needs to send you the response. That often reveals your location.

Then the code runs.

See, we’ve made a lot of civilizational progress in making browsing safe. [Long gone are the days when getting a virus just by visiting a website was a daily concern](https://www.darkreading.com/vulnerabilities-threats/browser-exploits-wane-users-become-attack-surface). The thing is, the definition of safety varies depending on who you ask. The broad consensus ends at isolation: a website’s code can’t see the data stored by other websites, and it can’t see your files or other applications without permission. **Chrome** and **Edge** stop here. Then you have **Safari** (especially on iOS/macOS 26+) and **Firefox** extending that definition to privacy, but they still don’t fully protect you from fingerprinting. **Brave** and **Tor** are the leading privacy-first browsers, with up and coming **Mullvad Browser** (Mullvad being, in my opinion, one of the best VPN providers out there).

The code runs on your hardware, which can be measured in ways that produce consistent and unique readings. There’s not much that can be done about this really, so there’s only two established solutions:

1.   feed a little bit of noise here and there. It’s called **farbling** and that’s what Brave does to make your fingerprint inconsistent.
2.   make everything look the same, always, so there’s no telling browser users apart. Tor and Mullvad adopt this approach.

## Ok, let’s create a fingerprint

So there are two sources for data that can make up your fingerprint; the network request and the code environment.

**When you look at network, the data is generally either fragile or generic:**

*   the IP address; in a ‘happy path’ where one person always uses the same IP address, it might be the only data you need. But commonly people do a lot of browsing on mobile networks, they share the WiFi with others, they use VPNs or their home network’s IP address is rotated by the ISP. It’s fragile as such.
*   headers like `User-Agent` or `Accept-Language`; reveal your browser, OS, versions and the language set.

**When you can execute code on the device, you have ways to measure its hardware qualities (without any permission prompts!) and these are surprisingly stable:**

*   GPU; behaviour, vendor, driver
*   CPU; behaviour, vendor, number of threads
*   memory size
*   display data; resolution, pixel ratio, refresh rate
*   audio processing
*   device model

**And on the software level; insta
fingerprints-are-the-new-cookies.background: Browser fingerprinting builds a unique profile from long‑lived device characteristics—such as installed fonts, screen resolution, and browser headers—to identify users without cookies. While useful for fraud detection, it is often deployed covertly to track visitors across sites, a practice that many users find disconcerting. In 2025, Google announced it would re‑introduce fingerprinting across its Chrome ecosystem, moving beyond the now‑controversial third‑party cookies and extending tracking to smart devices. The European Union’s GDPR treats fingerprinting as personal data, requiring explicit consent or a legitimate‑interest justification, and the ePrivacy Directive similarly mandates user notice.

total-annihilation-rebuilt-for-modern-co.title: Total Annihilation, rebuilt for modern computers
total-annihilation-rebuilt-for-modern-co.content:
Get closer.
Zoom in on your units and the action. See the familiar battlefield at a new scale.
Nanolathe / Open-source 2.5D RTS engine
Play the classic through a modern, MIT-licensed engine you can study, modify and build on.
Three original demo missions. No game folder or installation needed.
Desktop Chrome, Edge or Safari, with a keyboard and mouse.
Zoom in on your units and the action. See the familiar battlefield at a new scale.
Modern GPU rendering is the standard experience, with light, glow and richer detail. Prefer the old look? Switch to Classic.
Run natively on Windows, Mac or Linux, using the Total Annihilation game files you already own.
Play it. Understand it. Build on it.
Total Annihilation is Nanolathe’s starting point. Its code, documented formats and clean-room research are open for others to explore and extend.
A faithful foundation, modern rendering and a native beta for Windows, Mac and Linux.
Try the demoRead the game formats, study the engine’s design and follow the evidence behind its behavior.
Explore the engineModify the engine, experiment with mods or contribute to its next chapter. Nanolathe’s code is MIT licensed.
Code & contributionSame scene. Same instant.
See the tank catch the blast, glow spread across the scene, and grass and healthy trees gain detail. Drag to compare, or tap a view below.
Captured with engine 617540c5 on October 4, 2026. This compares full renderer paths: Modern includes supersampling and its default presentation effects. The tile cache was generated from the installed game’s original 32×32 tiles into real 64×64 synthesized tiles. Healthy tree sprites use real 2× synthesized feature banks; shadow or missing variants retain the engine’s normal fallback. Authored dead stumps are cleared from this staged display. No screenshot cropping, retouching or resampling was used. WebP exports decode to the exact captured pixels.
Your next battlefield.
Try three campaign missions in your browser. Install the beta with your own game data for full campaigns, skirmish and online play.
Desktop browsers for the demo.
Windows, Mac and Linux for the installed game.
A few things to know.
Nanolathe is an independent, MIT-licensed, open-source engine that reimplements Total Annihilation through clean-room research. It uses original game data supplied separately. It’s not affiliated with or endorsed by the game’s owners.
The browser demo includes the original three-mission demo, so you can try it without a game folder. To play the full game, bring the installed files from a copy you own, such as GOG, Steam or your original CDs. The engine’s MIT license applies to its code; Total Annihilation’s content is separate.
Single-player skirmish, Survival and campaign are broadly complete, and with your own game files you can play skirmish and Survival online with friends. Every skirmish and Survival battle is recorded as a replay. The beta still has bugs and smaller missing features; compatibility can vary by mission or content pack, and save compatibility is still being refined.
A desktop computer, keyboard and mouse. Chrome, Edge and Safari are supported desktop browsers. Firefox, mobile and tablet play have not been verified. Demo files download when you choose to play and are cached for your next visit. Install the beta for larger battles and the full native experience.
Yes, in the installed game or in desktop Chrome or Edge, and both can play together. Choose MULTI on the main menu to create a game and send its code to friends, or join with theirs. Skirmish takes 2 to 10 players, and Survival 2 or 3. The host chooses Modern, Community 3.9 or Strict 3.1 rules and can add computer players, and in battle you can chat, share and make alliances. Everyone needs their own game files; the three-mission demo can’t play online. Read the online guide.
The code and clean-room research are open to explore.
total-annihilation-rebuilt-for-modern-co.background: Nanolathe is an independent, MIT-licensed open-source engine that reimplements Total Annihilation through clean-room research. It allows players to experience the classic game on modern GPUs with enhanced lighting and detail while retaining options for a traditional look. The project runs natively on Windows, Mac, or Linux using original game files owned by the user without requiring installation for basic play. By studying documented formats and exploring open code, developers can modify the engine or build upon its foundation to create new content. This faithful recreation supports single-player campaigns and skirmishes while remaining unaffiliated with the original game's owners.

type-safe-html-templating-in-zig.title: Type-safe HTML templating in Zig
type-safe-html-templating-in-zig.background: The author has decades of web development experience spanning PHP, Python templates, and modern JavaScript frameworks before discovering Zig. While initially skeptical about low-level languages for frontend work, they realized that arena allocators and comptime make API backends manageable without manual deallocation. A critical gap remained in templating: the need for type safety to prevent runtime errors, zero allocations during output generation, built-in XSS protection via safe defaults, and a syntax resembling standard HTML rather than a foreign DSL. Unable to find an existing Zig solution meeting these criteria, the author adapted Templ (a Go library) into zt, which transpiles templates directly into typed Zig code that writes efficiently to std.Io.Writer sockets or buffers.

postgres-isn-t-slow-your-storage-is.title: Postgres isn't slow, your storage is
postgres-isn-t-slow-your-storage-is.content:
At POSETTE 2026, Sai Srirampur presented "Postgres Isn’t Slow. Your Storage Is." a talk examining how storage affects PostgreSQL performance at scale. This post recaps the benchmark, what the results revealed, and the architecture proposed for running PostgreSQL on local NVMe in production. You can watch the full talk in the video linked below.
The talk starts with several symptoms teams running Postgres at scale may recognize: ingestion slows down, P95 read latency becomes unpredictable, autovacuum falls behind, checkpoints compete with your actual workload for resources, or logical replication accumulates lag. These problems do not always share the same cause, but they can have a common one that is easy to overlook: storage performance.
To understand why, Sai ran a benchmark comparing the same 3.3-billion-row PostgreSQL workload on baseline gp3 EBS and local NVMe. We will walk through the setup and what Sai discovered when analyzing the results, then close with the production patterns proposed for running Postgres on local NVMe.
Five scaling symptoms
There are five common issues that often appear once a PostgreSQL workload reaches hundreds of gigabytes or terabytes and is running with real concurrency and throughput.
- 
Slow ingestion. The first one is ingestion pipelines heavy on UPDATEs and UPSERTs. Jobs that once finished in seconds can stretch into minutes as the volume of data underneath them grows. 
- 
Inconsistent read latency. Next one appears in workloads where most queries remain fast but a few become dramatically slower. P95 latency moves from milliseconds to seconds, dashboards time out, and the uneven slowdown makes the cause harder to isolate. 
- 
VACUUM falling behind. A third issue is autovacuum falling behind as UPDATE and UPSERT throughput grows, with table bloat accumulating from gigabytes into terabytes. 
- 
Slower checkpoints. Checkpoints can also take longer and compete with the client workload for I/O and CPU, turning an operation that used to be invisible into a recurring latency spike. 
- 
Logical replication lag. The last symptom appears when PostgreSQL data is streaming to systems such as Kafka or ClickHouse. WAL decoding can be slow and a growing replication slot can compound the problem. 
How do these symptoms connect to storage
As the working set outgrows the memory available to PostgreSQL and the operating-system page cache, more data read require physical I/O. On slower storage, the higher cost and queuing of those reads can increase both average and tail latency.
Client queries and background maintenance also use the same storage budget. Heap and index writes, WAL synchronization, checkpoints, VACUUM, and logical-decoding spills compete for bandwidth, IOPS, and queue capacity.
Once storage reaches one of those limits, operations begin delaying one another. That is how slow storage can be the root cause of several apparently unrelated PostgreSQL problems.
What changes with local NVMe
The case for local NVMe is not that it eliminates I/O, but that it can sharply reduce its cost. The comparison contrasts millisecond-scale operations on network-attached storage with operations that may complete in tens of microseconds on local NVMe. Cache misses, WAL flushes, and maintenance I/O still happen, but they simply don’t impact the overall system as much.
The benchmark: Local NVMe vs. EBS
To better understand why this is the case, Sai set up a simple experiment to compare a similar workload on PostgreSQL running on EBS and local NVMe.
Setup
To isolate storage as the variable, the benchmark used eight identical PostgreSQL clusters: four using instance-store NVMe and four using baseline gp3 EBS provisioned at 3,000 IOPS. Each cluster ran on an m6id.4xlarge instance with 16 vCPUs, 64 GiB of RAM, and 16 GiB of shared_buffers. We used multiple instances for each storage type to normalize variability across benchmark runs.
The setup used a 482 GiB pgbench_accounts heap containing 3.3 billion rows. Each cluster then ran the same highly concurrent random-UPDATE workload for five minutes, with 64 clients and 16 worker threads:
\set aid random(1, 3300000000)
UPDATE pgbench_accounts SET abalance = abalance + 1 WHERE aid = :aid;In short, the only difference between the two groups was the storage class.
What the benchmark showed
The benchmark produced a median 16,030 TPS for the NVMe clusters, compared with 1,734 TPS on EBS—a 9.24× difference in this test. Median transaction latency fell from 36.9 ms to 4.0 ms.
For different operations, NVMe completed a VACUUM over 10 GB of bloat in 366 seconds, compared with 964 seconds on EBS, and drained a 10 GB logical-replication backlog in 139 seconds instead of 238 seconds.
One qualification matters: these results apply to this workload and these storage configurations. The EBS side used baseline gp3 provisioned at 3,000 IOPS, different EBS setup would most likely produce different results.
Explaining the gap
The throughput gap becomes easier to understand by looking at where the 37 ms of EBS transaction latency went.
In this benchmark, page reads accounted for about 19 ms on EBS, compared with 0.3 ms on NVMe. WAL fsync at commit added another 11 ms on EBS versus 1.5 ms on NVMe, while lock and scheduler overhead contributed about 5 ms versus 0.2 ms. CPU work itself was roughly the same—about 2 ms in both cases.
In other words, most of the additional EBS latency came from waiting on storage, not from PostgreSQL doing more CPU work.
A mid-run pg_stat_activity snapshot showed the same pattern from another angle. Of the 64 backends, 29 on EBS were waiting on IO:DataFileRead, compared with nine on NVMe—roughly 45% versus 14%. This was a point-in-time snapshot rather than an average across the run, but it illustrates how many more EBS sessions were stalled on reads at that moment.
The CPU profile then adds a counterintuitive observation. Over a profiling window of roughly 240 seconds, the NVMe host accumulated 2,253 CPU-seconds—about 9.4 core
postgres-isn-t-slow-your-storage-is.background: At POSETTE 2026, Sai Srirampur presented "Postgres Isn't Slow. Your Storage Is," a talk examining how storage affects PostgreSQL performance at scale. The presentation highlights common symptoms teams face when running Postgres with large datasets and real concurrency, including slow ingestion, unpredictable P95 read latency, autovacuum lagging behind, delayed checkpoints, and logical replication accumulation. These issues often stem from a single overlooked cause: storage performance limitations rather than the database engine itself. As workloads grow beyond available memory and OS page cache, physical I/O costs on slower network-attached storage increase both average and tail latencies while competing for bandwidth and queue capacity with client queries and maintenance tasks. The talk proposes an architecture utilizing local NVMe to sharply reduce these operational costs by minimizing the impact of inevitable cache misses and WAL flushes compared to baseline EBS solutions.

whatever-became-of-holography-2011.title: Whatever became of holography? (2011)
whatever-became-of-holography-2011.content:
![Sigma XI](/sites/americanscientist.org/themes/amsci/img/sigma-xi-logo-sm.png)

# American Scientist

## Whatever Became of Holography?

### By [Sean F. Johnston](/author/sean_f._johnston)

The once-futuristic technology has less public glamour nowadays, but it still plays a current role in science

#### [Art](https://www.americanscientist.org/topics-names/Art) [Technology](https://www.americanscientist.org/topics-names/Technology) [Photography](https://www.americanscientist.org/free-tag-names/photography)

![Current Issue](https://www.americanscientist.org/sites/americanscientist.org/files/styles/issue_box_in_article/public/2011-99-6-cover.jpg?itok=FkzPPVk4)

### This Article From Issue

#### November-December 2011

##### Volume 99, Number 6

###### Page 482

DOI: [10.1511/2011.93.482](https://doi.org/10.1511/2011.93.482)

A generation ago, hologram exhibitions attracted hundreds of thousands of visitors in major cities around the world, and entrepreneurs confidently forecast applications in art, photography and television.

As holography became more ubiquitous, however, it lost some of its luster for public audiences as well as for professional scientists and engineers. But the technology still makes an impact today, although not with the same punch it had a quarter-century ago. Popular culture celebrates it through science fiction and a steady trickle of news reports about imminent consumer advances—although there are a number of modern instances where semi-transparent images of television announcers and pop stars are mislabeled as holograms, further confusing consumers who don’t understand what holograms are realistically capable of showing.

![](https://www.americanscientist.org/sites/americanscientist.org/files/2011101154318684-2011-11JohnstonF1.jpg)

Figure 1. Pioneering holographer Kenneth A. Haines uses a complicated laser setup to produce a hologram of the skull of Taung Child, a fossil that is over a million years old. Although the hologram was produced in the 1980s (it appeared on the cover of *National Geographic* in November 1985), the process is still typical for holograms of this type produced today. Holography may have peaked in popularity in past decades, but the technology is finding new uses in science.

**Jonathan Blair/National Geographic Stock**

The field that once represented futuristic progress gradually has been recast as a fertile technique at the heart of modern science, and ongoing research continues to pay dividends. But the science and technology may now seem old-hat. Where the field of digital electronics offers real-time, high-definition displays and three-dimensional television, much of holography remains stolidly analog. Audiences once amazed by lasers and stunningly realistic holograms have become jaded in the face of ubiquitous and unremarkable credit-card icons. And yet the history of this field illustrates some of the best science and most impressive technology of the past two generations. How did holography get to this point, and where might it be going?

The answers are often surprising even to many of the participants in the field, because holography has been continually fragmented between disciplines as distinct as art and electronics research, with some of this separation dating back to the end of World War II. For a subject often deemed unintuitive, it has been frequently reinvented: The field and its possibilities were conceived afresh for waves of successive audiences. Although holography remains a magical and inspirational field ripe with possibilities, it also demonstrates the dangers of unrefined forecasting and rosy visions of progress. Beyond the enduring fascination of the subject itself, holography provides important lessons for understanding the cultural factors behind scientific advances and technological change.

### Optical Groundwork

Although it came to represent high technology, holography was born from unlikely sources. The origins of technologies can be notoriously difficult to trace, but in this case there were at least three separate threads, in three countries, woven together to create the new subject. Those threads were tangled with others that had been conceived a generation or two earlier, or borrowed from neighboring fields. Each played a role in transforming a staid and unpopular science—optics—into a revolutionary subject at the forefront of late-20th-century physics.

By the end of World War II, optics had become a routine, if highly sophisticated, engineering field. *Geometrical optics*—the science of lens, camera and telescope design—was at the heart of important national industries, especially following the demands of wartime production. But relatively few physicists saw their future in a domain with such a heavy emphasis on applied technology. Its high-science counterpart, *physical optics*—dealing with wave phenomena such as interference and diffraction—had become a major research field during the late 19th century, but it had generated relatively little subsequent momentum in research and few practical applications.

![](https://www.americanscientist.org/sites/americanscientist.org/files/2011101155198685-2011-11JohnstonF2.jpg)

Figure 2. An early form of color photography, invented by Gabriel Lippmann, creates standing waves when light of different colors from a lens passes through the photographic emulsion and reflects from a mercury surface back into the emulsion. The waves darken the emulsion at points where the peaks of the incoming and reflected waves align (*dotted lines* ). When the processed plate is lit with white light, these darkened planes reinforce the original wavelength, creating color.

**Illustration by Tom Dunne.**

Only two such applications attracted much public attention. The first was an ingenious concept for color photography invented by French physicist Gabriel Lippmann during the 1890s. His technique used a fine-grained photographic emulsion to record light of different wavelengths a
whatever-became-of-holography-2011.background: Once a futuristic technology captivating global audiences with hologram exhibitions and promises for art and television, holography has gradually lost its public luster as it became more ubiquitous. While popular culture continues to celebrate the field through science fiction and occasional news reports of consumer advances, modern instances often mislabel semi-transparent images as true holograms, confusing consumers about their realistic capabilities. Although digital electronics now offer real-time high-definition displays, much of current holography remains stolidly analog despite its history illustrating impressive technology from the past two generations. The field has been continually fragmented between disciplines ranging from art to electronics research since World War II and is frequently reinvented for successive audiences seeking new applications in science rather than consumer gadgets.

calculus-with-julia.title: Calculus with Julia
calculus-with-julia.content:
Calculus with Julia
Preface
This is a set of notes for learning calculus using the Julia language. Julia is an open-source programming language with an easy to learn syntax that is well suited for this task.
Read “Getting started with Julia” to learn how to install and customize Julia for following along with these notes. Read “Julia interfaces” to review different ways to interact with a Julia installation.
Since the mid 90s there has been a push to teach calculus using many different points of view. The Harvard style rule of four says that as much as possible the conversation should include a graphical, numerical, algebraic, and verbal component. These notes use the programming language Julia to illustrate the graphical, numerical, and, at times, the algebraic aspects of calculus.
There are many examples of integrating a computer algebra system (such as Mathematica, Maple, or Sage) into the calculus conversation. Computer algebra systems can be magical. The popular WolframAlpha website calls the full power of Mathematica while allowing an informal syntax that is flexible enough to be used as a backend for Apple’s Siri feature. (“Siri what is the graph of x squared minus 4?”) For learning purposes, computer algebra systems model very well the algebraic/symbolic treatment of the material while providing means to illustrate the numeric aspects. These notes are a bit different in that Julia is primarily used for the numeric style of computing and the algebraic/symbolic treatment is added on. Doing the symbolic treatment by hand can be very beneficial while learning, and computer algebra systems make those exercises seem kind of redundant, as the finished product can be produced much more easily.
Our real goal is to get at the concepts using technology as much as possible without getting bogged down in the mechanics of the computer language. We feel Julia has a very natural syntax that makes the initial start up not so much more difficult than using a calculator, but with a language that has a tremendous upside. The notes restrict themselves to a reduced set of computational concepts. This set is sufficient for working many of the problems in calculus, but do not cover thoroughly many aspects of programming. (Those who are interested can go off on their own and Julia provides a rich opportunity to do so.) Within this restricted set, are operators that make many of the computations of calculus reduce to a function call of the form action(function, arguments...). With a small collection of actions that can be composed, many of the problems associated with introductory calculus can be attacked.
These notes are presented in pages covering a fairly focused concept, in a spirit similar to a section of a book. Just like a book, there are try-it-yourself questions at the end of each page. All have a limited number of self-graded answers. These notes borrow ideas from many sources, for example Strang (n.d.), Knill (n.d.), Schey (1997), Hass et al. (2018), Rogawski et al. (2019), Angenent (2012), several Wikipedia pages, and other sources.
These notes are accompanied by a Julia package CalculusWithJulia that provides some simple functions to streamline some common tasks and loads some useful packages that will be used repeatedly.
These notes are presented as a Quarto book. To learn more about Quarto books visit https://quarto.org/docs/books.
Compiling these notes into a pdf file with Quarto is possible with some piecing together of parts. The result is less than optimal and also quite large.
To contribute – say by suggesting additional topics, correcting a mistake, or fixing a typo – click the “Edit this page” link and join the list of contributors. Thanks to all contributors.
A very special thanks goes out to @fangliu-tju for their careful and most-appreciated proofreading and error spotting spread over a series of PRs.
Running Julia
For individual users Julia is installed quite easily with the juliaup utility or by other means. There are some brief installation notes in the overview of Julia commands.
Calculus with Julia version 0.27, produced on August 31, 2026.
calculus-with-julia.background: These notes serve as a set of materials for learning calculus using Julia, an open-source programming language noted for its easy syntax. Since the mid 90s, there has been a push to teach calculus through graphical, numerical, algebraic, and verbal components known as the Harvard style rule of four. While computer algebra systems like Mathematica offer symbolic power, these notes primarily use Julia for numeric computing with added algebraic treatment by hand. The goal is to grasp concepts using technology without getting bogged down in language mechanics, restricting computational concepts to a reduced set sufficient for introductory problems. These pages present focused concepts similar to book sections and include try-it-yourself questions with limited self-graded answers.

An editor and IDE for iPad with on-device LLM inference on an AMD GPU.
LemonSeed Studio is a single iPad app. It bundles:
- mac_linuxgpu: the
unmodified upstream Linux amdgpu+amdkfddriver, embedded in the app as a PCIDriverKit extension. It drives an AMD GPU in a Thunderbolt enclosure.
- LemonSeed Engine: the inference engine, running on that GPU through its HSA runtime and HRX/Loom.
- amdgpu_mtopg: live GPU telemetry.
third_party/mac_linuxgpu   GPU driver (submodule)
third_party/LSE            inference engine (submodule)
third_party/amdgpu_mtopg   GPU monitor (submodule)
git clone --recurse-submodules <repository>Or, in an existing clone:
git submodule update --initmac_linuxgpu fetches its own pinned Linux sources sparsely on first build, so its nested kernel submodule does not need to be cloned recursively.
The original code is available under MIT or GPL-2.0-only, at your option. See LICENSE. Bundled and submodule components keep their own licenses; see THIRD_PARTY.md.
running-the-unmodified-linux-amdgpu-driv.background: LemonSeed Studio is a single iPad application that functions as an editor and IDE by running unmodified upstream Linux amdgpu driver code directly on the device. This setup enables on-device large language model inference using an AMD GPU housed in a Thunderbolt enclosure via PCIDriverKit extensions. The app bundles its own LemonSeed Engine for HSA runtime execution, alongside live telemetry tools to monitor GPU performance. Components are sourced from third-party submodules and retain their original MIT or GPL-2.0-only licenses within the bundled distribution.

script.full_text:
Zod 4.6.6 was flagged for malware, but the package is actually clean.

Security researchers spotted a suspicious commit adding a pre-install script. Security teams across major registries have been on high alert following several supply chain attacks this year targeting widely used JavaScript libraries.

The script attempted to fetch and execute external code via JSON-RPC calls, specifically targeting a hardcoded IP address to download a payload. This pattern of injecting post-install scripts that phone home to external servers has become increasingly common in the npm ecosystem.

The change was reverted before publication, so the released npm version is safe.

And that's your security sorted. Now, imagine writing HTML in Zig.

A developer with decades of PHP and Python experience built type-safe templates in Zig. The language's built-in memory safety and zero-cost abstractions make it uniquely suited for performance-critical web rendering tasks.

Arena allocators and comptime make frontend work manageable without memory leaks.

With that covered -- here's a classic RTS reborn.

Nanolathe is an open-source engine reimplementing Total Annihilation for modern GPUs. It runs natively on Windows, Mac, or Linux using your existing game files.

Follow for daily tech news.
